analysis.one_liner: Requires pipeline companies to inspect and fix pipelines in populated areas and share hazard information with communities.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its House subcommittees and received no vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies that operate natural gas and hazardous liquid pipelines to test and inspect their pipelines where they run through densely populated areas and environmentally sensitive areas, and to fix problems they find. It would have raised the maximum civil penalty for violations from $500,000 to $1 million, made it easier to shut down a pipeline deemed hazardous, and given nearby communities more information — annual maps of where pipelines are located, public access to safety reports, and a national database of spill histories. It also strengthened state participation in overseeing interstate pipelines. The bill never advanced past its subcommittees and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near natural gas and hazardous liquid pipelines — especially in towns and cities — would gain stronger legal requirements that operators inspect, test, and repair pipes before they fail, plus more information about where pipelines run and what hazards they pose. Firefighters, local emergency planners, and state regulators would get better data, maps, and funding to respond to and investigate pipeline incidents.

how_it_helps.text: Required pipeline operators to assess risks where pipelines run through densely populated areas and environmentally sensitive areas, and to adopt integrity-management programs using internal inspection or equally protective pressure testing to find defects before they cause a failure.

Gave communities near pipelines more information: public education about release hazards, annual maps of pipeline locations provided to municipal governments, public access to safety reports and integrity-management information, and a national data repository of spill histories available to the public.

Strengthened enforcement: the Secretary could ask the Attorney General to shut down a hazardous facility in court, civil penalties rose from $25,000–$500,000 to $100,000–$1,000,000, and citizen suits could assess civil penalties against noncompliant operators.

Allowed states to enforce one-call excavation-damage-prevention requirements against interstate pipelines, let state authorities participate in federal oversight of interstate pipeline construction and incidents with federal funding, and required reporting of every release over five gallons.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline companies would bear the cost of inspections, integrity-management programs, higher penalties for violations, and mandatory reporting of releases. Excavators who dig without using the one-call notification system could face fines or a misdemeanor charge.

drawbacks.text: The bill put real compliance costs on pipeline operators, requiring periodic internal inspection or pressure testing of pipelines near populated areas, and raising the maximum civil penalty per violation from $500,000 to $1 million — costs that operators argued would ultimately flow into rates.

It created a new federal misdemeanor — up to one year in prison — for any person who excavates without first calling the one-call notification system, exposing ordinary contractors and landowners to criminal liability.

The bill relied heavily on future Transportation Department rulemaking with deadlines (final integrity-management regulations by December 31, 2000 for large operators), and an honest reader can note that deadlines in statutes are often missed, delaying the protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs were real but modest: pipeline companies would have paid for inspections, integrity programs, better public education, and potentially higher civil penalties, and the bill added a misdemeanor risk for careless excavators. Set against that, the bill targeted a specific, well-documented hazard — aging pipelines running near homes, schools, and waterways — and put information about those pipelines in the hands of the people who live near them. A supporter would honestly concede that the requirements were complex and compliance-heavy, and that some inspections on older uninspectable lines would have been redundant; but the core protections were reasonable and widely seen as overdue. On balance the benefits to the public outweighed the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to subcommittees, and stayed there — no hearings action, no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2000 by Representative Bud Shuster, a Republican, along with Ranking Member Jim Oberstar, a Democrat, and referred to both the Transportation and Infrastructure and Commerce Committees.

Within days it was sent to the House Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings, Hazardous Materials and Pipeline Transportation and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where it received no further action.
The bill never received a markup, a floor vote, or Senate action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so it died with that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators benefited by avoiding mandatory integrity testing, higher penalties, and new reporting near populated areas.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced on a bipartisan basis — a Republican chairman and the ranking Democrat — and there was no recorded vote to show how parties split; the opposition was the simple absence of committee action.

industries.industry: Natural gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: Operators would have borne new inspection, integrity-management, education, mapping, and reporting costs and higher penalties, but the requirements did not change their business model and arguably reduced the far larger costs of catastrophic failures. Their gain from the bill's death was avoiding mandatory integrity testing near populated areas.

The bill tightened penalties for not calling the one-call system before digging and created a new misdemeanor, while also clarifying that approved state one-call programs could substitute for federal rules — modest burden, clearer rules.

The bill expanded state authority to oversee interstate pipelines and authorized federal payment of up to 100 percent of state costs for special investigations, strengthening a public watchdog rather than an industry.
